frase_gancho.texto: The young god of flowers, his body covered in sacred plants.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the god of flowers we move on to his animal: the monkey, which the Mexica linked to dance and play. Now look for a small vessel of shiny black stone, shaped like a monkey.

guion_corto.texto: This young man of stone sits cross-legged, absorbed, as if in a trance. He is Xochipilli, “the Prince of Flowers,” god of flowers, music, dance, poetry, love and games. He stands a little over one meter tall and was found in Tlalmanalco, on the slopes of the Iztaccíhuatl volcano. Look closely at his body and at the throne where he sits: they are covered in reliefs of plants. There are flowers of wild tobacco, of a climbing vine called ololiuhqui, and of other plants that the Nahua peoples used in their rituals. On the pedestal, you will also find open-petaled flowers and butterflies drinking nectar. It is a sculpture that looks like a garden.

guion_largo.texto:
“Flower and song,” in xóchitl in cuícatl, meant poetry, art and, at bottom, truth in Nahuatl. For the Nahua, beauty was not a luxury but a path to touch the divine. Xochipilli was the god of that path. If in Teotihuacán the [Tepantitla mural](mna_s04_mural_tepantitla) showed a paradise of song among flowers, here that same spirit takes the form of a young man of stone.

His name breaks down into xóchitl, “flower,” and pilli, “prince” or “noble child”: the Prince of Flowers. He is also called Macuilxóchitl, “Five Flower,” the name of a day in the ritual calendar, and he is linked with the sign of the monkey, ozomatli, the sign of dance and play. You already glimpsed him on the side of the [Teocalli](mna_s06_teocalli_guerra_sagrada), among the gods who surround the eagle. According to myth, he was the son of Piltzintecuhtli and of Xochiquétzal, the goddess of love and flowers. At Tlaxochimaco, a festival of flower offerings, young people brought him marigold garlands, the same flower that today fills the altars for the dead.

His body is a herbarium. The sculptors carved specific flowers into his skin, such as those of wild tobacco, of the ololiuhqui and of the sinicuichi. The ololiuhqui is a climbing vine whose seeds produce visions; the sinicuichi, a yellow flower that was used in rituals. And among them, according to the scholar Gordon Wasson, one can see the caps of sacred mushrooms. This last point is still debated, but it fits with what the chronicles say, which speak of teonanácatl, “flesh of the gods.”

We should not imagine all this as a party. For the Nahua, those plants were sacred and were used with ceremony, above all in the rituals of priests and sages, the tlamatinime, “those who know.” The Spanish friars condemned these practices. The statue reminds us that Mexica religion was also a very refined knowledge of nature: plants that heal, that alter the mind, that open the senses.

This idea is found in Nahua poems. They speak of life as a flower that withers and of poetry as the only thing that endures. Verses are attributed to Nezahualcóyotl, the poet king of Texcoco, saying that even jade shatters and gold breaks, but that song goes on. If Tízoc wanted to be remembered for his conquests, the poets believed that what endures is beauty.

It was found in the early nineteenth century in Tlalmanalco, in the Chalco region, at the foot of the Iztaccíhuatl. That area had celebrated stonecutters, and some think the sculpture came from Chalca hands. After its discovery, it became part of the collection of the historian Alfredo Chavero, who at first took it for another god, Izcozauhqui, and later identified it correctly. It passed to the old National Museum, on Moneda Street, and in 1964 it arrived here.

When you look at it from the front, think about the contrast. This hall began with a goddess in a skirt of serpents and with another, dismembered goddess; here it is time to see the other side. The Mexica were capable of both things: war and tenderness. Whoever tells you they were only blood and stone has not looked closely at this sculpture.

texto.Dimensions: 117 cm high x 55 cm wide x 45 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Xochipilli was the “god of drugs” of the Mexica.
texto.respuesta: Reality: He was the god of flowers, music, dance, poetry and play. The plants on his body speak of sacred rituals, not of recreation.
